question: Before farming, how did people get, cook and burn fat — and what do the oldest traces of it show?
thesis: Before farming, fat is the prize of hunting and the evidence is of work: Neanderthals boil bones for grease, hunters choose the fattest animals, and the first pots on three coasts cook fish. Plant fat is gathered rather than pressed; the dairy herd and the oil crops belong to the next folio.

big_ideas.title: Fat was worth the labour
big_ideas.text: The oldest clear sign of fat processing is rendering: Neanderthals crush the bones of at least 172 large animals and boil out the grease, and Levantine hunters break gazelle bones for marrow. Recorded hunters’ practice and explorers’ accounts of lean meat explain why: people choose the fattest animals and suffer without grease.

big_ideas.title: Water gave fat early
big_ideas.text: Shellfish and perhaps beached blubber at Pinnacle Point, Nile fish at Wadi Kubbaniya and the aquatic oils in the first pots of Japan and the Amur show that sea and river were fat sources from very early, long before any herd.

big_ideas.title: Fat becomes a technology: lamp and pot
big_ideas.text: Animal fat burns in the stone lamps of Lascaux, and the first pots, from China, Japan and the Amur, are where lipids survive to show what was cooked. Light and cooking are the first uses of fat that go beyond eating it raw.

big_ideas.title: Plant fat is gathered, not pressed
big_ideas.text: Wild olives, almonds and pistachios at Ohalo II, heaps of oleaster stones, the mongongo nut of the Kalahari and the avocado of the Americas show tree and nut fats in use, but none is shown to have been pressed. Where there were few herds, small prey such as grubs and termites supplied fat.

threads.title: Grease and marrow: fat from large animals
threads.claim: The earliest evidence is of rendering and marrow-breaking, and later recorded practice shows what it served.

beats.text: Neanderthals at Neumark-Nord crush the bones of at least 172 large mammals and heat the fragments in water to render grease.
Stone lamps at Lascaux and elsewhere burn animal fat.
In the Levant the shape of gazelle assemblages is explained by intensive marrow and grease extraction.
Northern hunters, in recorded practice, crack bones for marrow, boil out ‘bone juice’ and make akutuk and pemmican.
Prehistoric Aleut hunters prefer the fattest sea lions, and bison remains show selection of the fattest individuals.
Explorers’ accounts say it is nearly as hard to live on lean meat without grease as to starve.

threads.title: Fat from water, and the first pots
threads.claim: Shore and river provide fat from the Cape coast to the Nile, and the first pottery cooks aquatic food.

beats.text: At Pinnacle Point, South Africa, people eat shellfish, and a whale barnacle is read as a sign of scavenged blubber.
The first pots in China are used for cooking, though what they held is unknown.
Nile fishers at Wadi Kubbaniya process fish on the dunes at the flood.
Pots on the lower Amur cook fish oils, those on the middle Amur ruminant fat.
Japan’s Incipient Jōmon pots boil freshwater and marine animals, in the earliest pots with lipid evidence.

threads.title: Plant and small-prey fat, gathered
threads.claim: Trees, nuts and insects are fat sources too, though no pressing is shown before the next folio.

beats.text: Heaps of wild olive stones lie in Palaeolithic and Neolithic sites around the Mediterranean.
Ohalo II on the Sea of Galilee holds wild olives, almonds and pistachios among 90,000 plant remains.
The mongongo nut, 58 per cent fat, is a staple of the Kalahari San.
Palm grubs, winged termites and the Bogong moth supply fat in accounts from Africa, New Guinea and Australia.
Avocado stones turn up in Peru, Colombia, Honduras and Mexico.

turning_points.text: Shellfish and perhaps whale blubber at Pinnacle Point: the sea as a food source.
Neanderthals render bone grease at scale at Neumark-Nord.
Wild olives, almonds and pistachios are gathered at Ohalo II.
Levantine hunters break gazelle bones for marrow and grease.
The first pots appear in China.
Amur pots cook fish oils and ruminant fat.
Japan’s Jōmon pots boil aquatic food.
Avocado stones in four countries of the Americas.

text: The two European sites: the bone-grease works at Neumark-Nord and the fat lamps of Lascaux and other caves ([[te1]], [[te2]]).

Three entries: gazelle bones broken for grease in the Levant, the oily wild fruits and nuts of Ohalo II, and the Nile fishers of Wadi Kubbaniya ([[ec4]], [[ec5]], [[ec7]]). Egypt is filed here by the atlas taxonomy, though Wadi Kubbaniya is African. The first butter begins in the next folio.

Three entries: the Jōmon pots of Japan, whose lipids show aquatic cooking; the Amur pots, with fish oils on the lower river and ruminant fat on the middle; and China’s Xianrendong pots, whose contents are unknown ([[ec1]], [[ec8]], [[te3]]). India has no entry; the search found nothing.

Two entries: shellfish and perhaps beached-whale blubber at Pinnacle Point, from a paper read ([[ec6]]), and the fats of the Kalahari San, recorded in the 1960s and used here only as context ([[ec9]]). Nothing in the library covers African Stone Age marrow, grease or lamps, though the continent is where our species began.

Three entries: marrow, bone juice and pemmican among northern hunters; the Aleut and bison hunters’ choice of the fattest animals; and avocado stones at four sites from Peru to Mexico by 9000 BC ([[ec2]], [[th1]], [[ec10]]). Two are recorded practice, not Palaeolithic finds.
No entry. The first tree-crop evidence from Near Oceania is in the next folio.

The wild olive stones of the Mediterranean basin, a range spanning three continents; Speth’s explorers’ accounts from North America and East Africa; and the insect-eaters of Africa, New Guinea and Australia in Kiple ([[ec3]], [[th2]], [[th3]]).

sources.intro: This folio rests on recent archaeological papers read in full (Marean 2007, Wu 2012, Shoda 2020, VanDerwarker 2025), on books (Speth, Lee & DeVore, Bar-Yosef & Valla, Kiple), and on web summaries where the paper was not read (Neumark-Nord, Lascaux, the Jōmon pots, the gazelle studies, Ohalo II, Wadi Kubbaniya).
main: Marean et al. 2007, Wu et al. 2012, Shoda et al. 2020 and VanDerwarker et al. 2025 ([[ec6]], [[te3]], [[ec8]], [[ec10]]); Bar-Yosef & Valla (eds.) for the el-Wad bone breakage ([[ec4]]).

Speth for the explorers’ accounts ([[th2]]); Lee & DeVore for the Kalahari San ([[ec9]]); Kiple for marrow, pemmican, the choice of fat animals, the avocado’s place and insects as a fat food ([[ec2]], [[th1]], [[ec10]], [[th3]]); Mueller for the wild olive ([[ec3]]).

Web summaries of Kindler et al. 2025, the Lascaux page, Craig et al. 2013 and Munro & Bar-Oz ([[te1]], [[te2]], [[ec1]], [[ec4]]); university and museum pages for Ohalo II and Wadi Kubbaniya ([[ec5]], [[ec7]]).
contested: The Neumark-Nord ‘fat factory’ is the press’s framing of one paper ([[te1]]); the start of fat lamps at 40,000 years comes from a hobbyist page ([[te2]]); the Pinnacle Point blubber is the authors’ tentative suggestion from one barnacle fragment ([[ec6]]).

The marrow, fat-selection, Kalahari, explorers, Nile-fish and Xianrendong entries are CONTEXT: recorded practice, an argument, or a find with no fat evidence ([[ec2]], [[th1]], [[ec9]], [[th2]], [[ec7]], [[te3]], [[th3]]); the avocado finds are about domestication, not fat ([[ec10]]).
gaps: India has no entry: the search for Palaeolithic or Mesolithic fat processing on the subcontinent found nothing, and Fuller’s South Asian synthesis (now read) starts only with Neolithic Mehrgarh; the Indian record before farming may simply be thin.

Africa has two entries, one of them recorded practice; nothing on Stone Age African marrow and grease sites. China has only the soot-marked pots, with no residue; Korea, the Arctic and the Pacific coasts, and plant fats such as nuts, which leave little trace, are not covered. Moseley’s book on Andean maritime foundations, added to the folder as a djvu file, has not yet been read.

how_to_read: Read the thesis and the big ideas first, then the threads: each runs in date order and points to the entries that carry it. Entries that no thread needs are still reached through the regional picture and the lists.

Sixteen entries, so read straight through. The *picture by region* counts the 16 entries: Europe 2, Near East 3, Far East 3, Africa 2, Americas 3, Worldwide 3; none in Oceania. Dates are very approximate: several are placeholders or brackets from a period name or a recorded practice. India is a blank because the search found nothing.
The next folio starts at 8000 BC with the first butter and the first crops pressed for oil.
